AST SpaceMobile Is Down 55% in 2026: Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up? ©@Seasonal via Canva, @Oleksii Mach via Canva
Key Takeaways

AST SpaceMobile is down 55% in 2026 and hit a new 52-week low on Nov. 6, after a $1.15 billion convertible raise in July and SpaceX's push into direct-to-phone service.

SpaceX's spectrum buy and its reported talks to buy Boost Mobile could put Starlink up against AT&T and AST's other carrier partners.

AST trades well below its usual forward sales multiple, but its cash barely exceeds the burn analysts expect through 2028, and its new rocket adds about $900 million in cash costs on top.

Every $1 billion of new stock now takes about four times as many shares as at the May high, so the Nov. 9 report needs firm launch dates that make another raise less likely.

AST SpaceMobile (ASTS:NASDAQ) is down 55% in 2026. It hit a 52-week low of $27.58 on Nov. 6 before closing at $32.33, about three-quarters below its May high.

SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) went public in June. Since then it has agreed to buy spectrum and, reportedly, gone after a US network that could let Starlink sell phone service against AT&T (T:NYSE), AST's lead US carrier partner.

SpaceX keeps closing in

On Oct. 8, SpaceX agreed to buy Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz spectrum, airwaves AST had reportedly pursued too. On Nov. 2, The Washington Post reported that SpaceX is in talks to buy EchoStar's Boost Mobile, or to use its network, though neither has confirmed it. And SpaceX's Falcon 9 flew AST's last two BlueBird missions, so for now AST relies on its biggest competitor to reach orbit.

That's awkward for AT&T, which needs AST's satellites up before Starlink reaches its customers' phones. On Nov. 2, the two companies said they'd completed what they believe is the first handoff between a ground network and AST's satellites. AT&T also leases capacity to Boost and, per the Post, may need to approve moving those leases to SpaceX, giving it a say over Starlink's US plans.

AST's own schedule slipped too

In July, AST pushed back its goal of roughly 45 BlueBirds in orbit to early 2027, from late 2026. It has launched 13, one of them lost in April. Those satellites have to fly before revenue can grow from $70.9 million in 2025 to the $1.73 billion analysts expect for 2028:

Analysts' 2027 estimate is already down to $609 million, from $748 million on June 30, and another delay would likely bring more cuts.

Key Takeaways

Jim Cramer told a Mad Money caller on Friday to sell AT&T. He did it two days after Qualcomm said SpaceX picked it to power Starlink Mobile's nationwide 5G network.

AT&T and T-Mobile are reportedly ready to cut Boost Mobile off their networks if SpaceX buys it, a sign the carriers see a fourth network as a threat to their pricing.

Wireless made 96.9% of AT&T's segment operating income in 2025, and analysts expect its revenue to grow under 2% a year through 2028.

Verizon trades at 8.8x forward earnings, near its three-year average, so the big three have little cushion if SpaceX pushes wireless prices down, and AT&T is one to avoid for now.

Jim Cramer has a simple message for AT&T (T:NYSE) shareholders worried about SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ): Sell.

On Friday's episode of Mad Money, a caller asked for his take on AT&T "with the emergence of SpaceX and all the new technology out there." Cramer's answer:

"I think that Elon Musk is a vicious competitor. I think AT&T represents old and he represents new. So I am going to say you should not own AT&T."

He said he has Starlink in Europe, where he swapped a $150 system for a $50 one that he called much better and much faster. He also called his answer a "tough call." This week's news makes it a little easier.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on AT&T, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See AT&T's Analyst Ratings

The carriers are already playing defense

SpaceX's interest in Boost Mobile looked like a shortcut into wireless when The Washington Post reported the talks. SpaceX would buy Boost or get access to its network, which Boost leases from AT&T and T-Mobile.

On Wednesday, the push got more concrete. On Qualcomm (QCOM:NASDAQ)'s fiscal fourth-quarter call, CEO Cristiano Amon said "SpaceX selected Qualcomm to power Starlink Mobile's nationwide terrestrial 5G network in the U.S." Deployment begins in 2027 under a multiyear agreement, and Amon expects it to be one of the largest 5G rollouts in the country. That gives SpaceX the equipment for a credible fourth national network. It also gives Qualcomm what Amon called "a significant win for our infrastructure business."

A day later, Semafor's Rohan Goswami reported, citing sources, that AT&T and T-Mobile will kick Boost off their spectrum if Musk goes ahead with a takeover.

You don't threaten to cut off a customer over a rival you aren't worried about.

'Big Short' investor Steve Eisman says America's three biggest wireless carriers are no longer worth owning as Elon Musk's SpaceX prepares to challenge their dominance.

"I think the big three are just uninvestable," Eisman said on the Nov. 6 episode of The Real Eisman Playbook, just three weeks after calling the threat "probably overblown."

His warning followed SpaceX's Nov. 4 deal with Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) to supply technology for tens of thousands of 5G cell sites, with deployment beginning in 2027.

From 'Overblown' to 'Uninvestable'

On Oct. 16, Eisman called the telecom selloff a "telepocalypse," but said the threat was likely overdone. Building a conventional network would be extraordinarily expensive, he argued, although he warned that "narratives are powerful."

He noted that T-Mobile (NASDAQ:TMUS) traded at around 14 times projected 2026 earnings, down from a multiple in the 20s.

A week later, Eisman flagged the risk to SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), warning that Starlink's expansion could turn it from a "cash cow" into a "cash drain."

By Oct. 30, he was calling T-Mobile's strong earnings "largely irrelevant," arguing that Musk's ambitions mattered more to investors than current profits.

By then, SpaceX was reportedly seeking access to at least 80,000 U.S. cell sites, including through talks with Crown Castle. Days later, reports emerged SpaceX was exploring a deal with Boost Mobile's parent, EchoStar, to acquire the carrier or gain access to its network.

The danger extends beyond losing subscribers. A cheaper fourth carrier could force AT&T (NYSE:T) and Verizon (NYSE:VZ), along with T-Mobile, to cut prices across millions of existing customers, squeezing margins while their expensive networks remain in place.

Can Musk Really Challenge the Big Three?

Telecom expert William Webb told Benzinga that investors were overreacting. He estimated the immediate threat justified only a 1% to 2% cut to T-Mobile's valuation, rather than 7% to 15%.

Webb estimated SpaceX could need another $120 billion to $130 billion to approach the incumbents' nationwide capabilities, including substantial spectrum purchases.

Roger Entner of Recon Analytics told Benzinga that a narrower, rural-first network could cost $10 billion to $15 billion, excluding spectrum.

"He plays where he's strong and the other guys are weak," Entner said.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket traders give SpaceX a 21% chance of launching a qualifying U.S. mobile service by June 2027 and 53% by December 2027, with roughly $46,000 traded.

title: These 6 Telecom Stocks Collect Monthly Bills No Matter What the Market Does
detail:
These 6 Telecom Stocks Collect Monthly Bills No Matter What the Market Does
James Brumley, The Motley Fool
Mon, November 9, 2026 at 8:20 AM CST 7 min read
T
VZ
TMUS
CMCSA
CHTR
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Most investors are willing to take the occasional swing on a risky growth stock. The fact is, however, companies like AT&T (NYSE: T), Verizon Communications (NYSE: VZ), T-Mobile US (NASDAQ: TMUS), Comcast (NASDAQ: CMCSA), Charter Communications (NASDAQ: CHTR), and Lumen Technologies (NASDAQ: LUMN) are the kinds of companies that provide the reliable results that investors need.

Their common thread? They're all telecom names with businesses that generate regular revenue from customers paying monthly bills to maintain these connections...at least for the time being. In some of these cases, that could be changing soon.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Here's a closer look at each one and what the foreseeable future holds.

1. AT&T

There was a time when AT&T was not only the biggest and best-known name in the telecom business, but also its best investment. That's not the case anymore, though. With 110.2 million total subscribers (91.7 million of which are phone subscribers), AT&T is now technically behind Verizon and T-Mobile in terms of total wireless market share.

It didn't necessarily have to be this way. AT&T arguably just tried too hard to expand into arenas it thought would be more natural fits. It acquired satellite cable brand DirecTV in 2015, for instance, and then scooped up entertainment powerhouse Time Warner in 2018. Both businesses have since been shed, but at a loss that's still echoing. The company stopped raising its dividend in 2022, aiming to shore up a relatively ugly balance sheet. Although its customers still pay their bills like clockwork, AT&T still has a great deal of work to do to become a top-tier investment again.

2. T-Mobile

Some investors are surprised to learn that T-Mobile, rather than Verizon, is the nation's single-biggest wireless service provider in terms of customer headcount, with 142 million paying customers. Just remember this figure also includes all of the customers that came over from Sprint when the two companies were combined in 2020.

It's been a pretty solid performer too, although not unlike AT&T, its foray into the cable television business with what ended up being launched as TVision in 2019 was probably ill-advised. Meanwhile, it remains to be seen if its at-home wireless internet endeavor will pay off in the long run, although, as of the latest disclosure, there are over 8 million of these broadband customers. Not bad.

3. Verizon

Finally, quietly nestled in between T-Mobile and AT&T is Verizon, which has remained more focused on its core telecom business, investing money where it matters the most, like its fiberoptic network that supports its home-broadband business as well as its wireless operation. It has 11 million traditional fiber-broadband customers, and more than 6 million wireless home-broadband subscribers in addition to its massive mobile phone customer base.

This focus -- paired with capital spending with the biggest ROI -- has been well worth it too. During its recently ended fiscal Q3, the company experienced its strongest third-quarter of postpaid phone customer growth since 2021, and its highest net growth in total accounts in over a decade, prompting Verizon to raise its full-year revenue guidance for a third straight quarter.

Image source: Getty Images.

Shareholders are benefiting from this resiliency in an immediate way as well, with this stock's dividend. It's now been raised for 20 consecutive years, reflecting the company's ongoing growth. You can plug into this ticker while its forward-looking yield stands at 6.2%, which is the highest among the three mobile telecom names in focus here.

4. Comcast

Technically speaking, Comcast's Xfinity brand is in the wireless telecom business too, with 10.6 million subscribers as of the end of September. It's also parent to television broadcast network NBC and film studio Universal. Its breadwinning businesses are still cable TV and broadband service, though, which account for roughly two-thirds of its quarterly revenue of just under $20 billion.

And that's a problem. For a long while, the growth of its broadband business could offset the slow attrition of cable customers due to cord-cutting. Now that's not even happening. That's why Comcast's overall revenue hasn't grown in years.

Data source: Comcast Corp. Chart by author.

It's not necessarily the end of the world just yet. Total revenue isn't shrinking either. Customers still need to keep their connections active, and the company is still turning more than enough of their monthly payments into profits, which in turn supports its dividend payment.

For the first time in a long time, though, Comcast didn't raise its per-share payout at the beginning of this year. It may be a hint that the long-term sustainability of its business has reached a tipping point.

5. Charter Communications

You may know Charter Communications better by its operating brand name Spectrum, which offers cable television and broadband internet service, although, like Comcast, it's also easing into the wireless telecom arena. It was serving 13.5 million mobile customers as of the end of September, which is roughly one-third of its total 36.7 million customer relationships.

Like Comcast, this pure(r) telecommunications name had been able to offset the impact of the cord-cutting movement with the addition of broadband subscribers. That's not working anymore, however. Revenue has stagnated, even if it continues to flow. Ditto for earnings.

But does it offer a solid dividend until then? Nope, Charter has never paid a dividend, and isn't apt to start now. Instead, it has used its earnings to fund stock buybacks, which does add shareholder value. There's no particularly beneficial endgame in sight for shareholders, however. The company is just mitigating how its business is fading away.

6. Lumen Technologies

Last but not least, Lumen Technologies is one of a handful of telecom outfits with reliable revenue from its customers' monthly bill payments. Just not in the way you might imagine.

It's not a household name. That's because it doesn't serve consumer households. Rather, Lumen offers networking solutions specifically built for artificial intelligence platforms.

The company's near future isn't entirely clear. Although its third-quarter total revenue fell to $2.7 billion, its strategic revenue improved 10% year over year to $1.28 billion thanks to a 24% quarter-to-quarter increase in active customers. It's per-share loss was pared back from $0.20 to a loss of only $0.14 per share this time around, but Lumen shrank its way to that progress.

A bet on Lumen Technologies is still ultimately a bet on the continued proliferation of AI data centers, though, and the subsequent need to make them safer, faster, and more efficient. Just be patient as it makes this transition. It's expected to report slightly lower revenue again next year, as it continues to chip away at its losses.

Quick test: a dividend is sustainable when the right earnings base covers it (AFFO or FFO for REITs, EPS for ordinary companies), when free cash flow pays for it after capital spending, and when the company isn't taking on more debt to keep the checks going out. AT&T (T): Leverage Jumps as the Stock Slides

AT&T pays $1.11 a year, which works out to a 5.1% forward yield at $21.63. Shares are down 8.68% year to date. Management has committed to keeping the payout at $1.11 through 2028.

Net debt to adjusted EBITDA rose to 3.13x from 2.68x after the $23 billion EchoStar spectrum purchase. Management doesn't expect to get back to its 2.5x target until 2029. Third-quarter free cash flow of $4.95B fell 5.93%, and dividends plus buybacks used $4.753B of it. Legacy copper revenue dropped 24.5%. Wall Street Analysts Believe Tutor Perini (TPC) Could Rally 30.6%: Here's is How to Trade
Zacks Equity Research

Tutor Perini (TPC) closed the last trading session at $89.89, gaining 7.8% over the past four weeks, but there could be plenty of upside left in the stock if short-term price targets set by Wall Street analysts are any guide. The mean price target of $117.4 indicates a 30.6% upside potential.

The average comprises five short-term price targets ranging from a low of $107.00 to a high of $125.00, with a standard deviation of $6.8. While the lowest estimate indicates an increase of 19% from the current price level, the most optimistic estimate points to a 39.1% upside. More than the range, one should note the standard deviation here, as it helps understand the variability of the estimates. The smaller the standard deviation, the greater the agreement among analysts.

While the consensus price target is a much-coveted metric for investors, solely banking on this metric to make an investment decision may not be wise at all. That's because the ability and unbiasedness of analysts in setting price targets have long been questionable.

However, an impressive consensus price target is not the only factor that indicates a potential upside in TPC. This view is strengthened by the agreement among analysts that the company will report better earnings than what they estimated earlier. Though a positive trend in earnings estimate revisions doesn't give any idea as to how much the stock could surge, it has proven effective in predicting an upside.

Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise
Zacks Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise Chart for TPC
Here's What You May Not Know About Analysts' Price Targets

According to researchers at several universities across the globe, a price target is one of many pieces of information about a stock that misleads investors far more often than it guides. In fact, empirical research shows that price targets set by several analysts, irrespective of the extent of agreement, rarely indicate where the price of a stock could actually be heading.

While Wall Street analysts have deep knowledge of a company's fundamentals and the sensitivity of its business to economic and industry issues, many of them tend to set overly optimistic price targets. Are you wondering why?

They usually do that to drum up interest in shares of companies that their firms either have existing business relationships with or are looking to be associated with. In other words, business incentives of firms covering a stock often result in inflated price targets set by analysts.

However, a tight clustering of price targets, which is represented by a low standard deviation, indicates that analysts have a high degree of agreement about the direction and magnitude of a stock's price movement. While that doesn't necessarily mean the stock will hit the average price target, it could be a good starting point for further research aimed at identifying the potential fundamental driving forces.

Verizon Communications Inc. VZ has increased 14.7% in a year compared with the Wireless National industry's growth of 105.6%. The stock has outformed the Zacks Computer & Technology sector during this period.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

The company has outperformed its peers like AT&T Inc. T and T-Mobile US, Inc. TMUS. Shares of AT&T have declined 12.9%, while T-Mobile has declined 21.3% during this period.

Key Growth Drivers for Verizon

Verizon's improving wireless subscriber momentum is emerging as a major driver of its growth. In the third quarter of 2026, the company added 406,000 postpaid phone customers, marking its strongest third-quarter performance in five years. Postpaid account net additions reached 137,000, the highest quarterly performance in more than a decade. At the same time, postpaid phone churn improved to 0.94%, down 4 basis points year over year.

Moreover, Verizon reduced its promotional customer acquisition and retention costs by 41% and 30%, respectively. The combination of higher subscriber additions, lower churn and reduced customer acquisition expenses reflects an improvement in customer economics. Encouraged by these trends, management raised its 2026 postpaid phone net addition target to 1.1-1.2 million from the previous range of 750,000-1 million.

Broadband expansion and the growing adoption of converged services provide another important growth opportunity. Verizon added 314,000 broadband subscribers in the third quarter, taking its total broadband connections to approximately 17.4 million. Verizon remains on track to exceed 32 million fiber passings by the end of 2026, with a longer-term target of 40-50 million. The integration of Frontier Communications is expanding Verizon's fiber footprint and creating additional opportunities to cross-sell wireless and broadband services. Management noted that customers subscribing to both services demonstrate lower churn than single-product customers, supporting higher customer lifetime value.

AI infrastructure represents an emerging source of revenue diversification for Verizon. The company has signed a dark fiber agreement worth more than $2 billion with Amazon Web Services (AWS), building on its earlier agreement with Google to connect AI data centers. Management disclosed approximately $4 billion in signed contracts, supported by growing demand from hyperscalers, neocloud providers and enterprise customers.

Major Challenges for Verizon

Intensifying competition in the U.S. wireless and broadband markets remains a significant concern for Verizon. The company faces strong competition from AT&T, T-Mobile and cable operators, which continue to use competitive pricing, promotional incentives and bundled offerings to attract subscribers. Although Verizon has recently improved customer acquisition and retention metrics, sustaining subscriber growth without increasing promotional spending will be important. Its strategy of competing through network quality, customer experience and value-added services rather than aggressive price discounts could help protect margins. However, competitors adopting similar convergence strategies or increasing promotional activity could put pressure on Verizon's subscriber growth and pricing flexibility.

Weakness in equipment revenue is another challenge for the company. While mobility and broadband service revenue increased 2.9% year over year to $23.5 billion in the third quarter, lower equipment sales limited overall revenue growth. Total revenue increased just 1.5% to $34.3 billion, as equipment revenue declined 9% year over year. Management attributed the decline primarily to a reduction in wireless device upgrade activity, with postpaid upgrade volumes falling 20.3% from the prior-year quarter.

Verizon's substantial investment requirements and elevated debt remain important considerations. The company continues to allocate significant capital toward fiber deployment, wireless spectrum, network modernization and AI infrastructure. Its 2026 capital expenditure outlook remains at $16-$16.5 billion. Verizon reported total debt of $166.2 billion at the end of the third quarter, compared with $146.8 billion a year earlier. Net unsecured debt stood at $123.7 billion, while its net unsecured debt-to-adjusted EBITDA ratio was 2.3X. High debt burden may limit financial flexibility and leave very little room for execution related obstacles.

title: If I Could Give My Younger Self 1 Piece of Investing Advice, This Is What It Would Be
detail:
If I Could Give My Younger Self 1 Piece of Investing Advice, This Is What It Would Be
Alex Carchidi, The Motley Fool

T

Trading disclosure

If I could give my younger self one piece of investing advice, I'd find most of the material I'd need by reviewing my first-ever investment. My first stock was Lucent Technologies, which in 1996 was spun off from AT&T, and then bought by me at age 10 with all $500 of the birthday money I had saved up from prior years. Shortly after my purchase in late 1999, it began a long decline that saw its price fall 99.2% by September 2002.

The sting of that collapse kept me away from investing for about 15 years. So here's the investing advice that I would give to my younger self if I had to do things over again -- it's one central theme, and it has three parts.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
1. Don't put all your eggs in one basket

This advice seems obvious now, but new investors still need to learn it.

Funneling all your capital into one stock means one failure can wipe out most of your portfolio. Per research conducted at Arizona State University, about 4.3% of the nearly 26,000 U.S. stocks included in the analysis accounted for nearly all of the market's wealth creation above Treasury bills from 1926 to 2016. That's an argument for owning a large and diversified basket of stocks via an index fund like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO).

The lesson extends to the types of assets you invest in, too. The traditional 60/40 stocks/bonds portfolio split is timeless because holding bonds can make up for underperformance that stocks experience under certain conditions, and vice versa. Today, adding some cryptocurrency into your portfolio is another way to diversify even beyond that.

2. Accept that some eggs won't ever hatch

If you invest in a lot of different companies, some of those investments will not play out.

According to a 2014 J.P. Morgan study, 40% of Russell 3000 index stocks from 1980 to 2014 ended up experiencing a catastrophic loss, which in this case is defined as a 70% or larger drop from the peak with little recovery afterward. In the case of my first investment, in the telecom industry, the catastrophic loss rate was 51%.

The bigger point here is psychological in nature. Expecting every one of your stock picks to work out is not reasonable, but investing requires us to be rationally hopeful each time. The truth is that failure in investing is inevitable, and vastly more common than success. Quitting after the first big failure, as I did, cost me years of compounding, and not having the proper context to process the defeat in a constructive way was especially deleterious.
